content: 1. Nutrition Plans and Implementation of HIV and Infant Feeding Protocols: National HIV and infant feeding plans are implemented in various ways, including as stand-alone protocols or integrated into broader frameworks such as Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF), HIV/PMTCT (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission), or general nutrition protocols. Some countries do not have specific plans in place. 2. Postpartum Follow-Up for Mothers Living with HIV and Their Infants: In approximately 75% of surveyed countries, more than half of clinics and hospitals are effectively implementing comprehensive PMTCT programs, including antiretroviral (ARV) therapy and postnatal support. National protocols for infant ARV prophylaxis commonly include six weeks of nevirapine (NVP) for infants. Other variations include 12 weeks of NVP, combinations of NVP and zidovudine (AZT), or adjustments based on infant HIV status or maternal treatment history. 3. Special Recommendations for Infant ARV Prophylaxis: Adjustments to ARV regimens are made in specific cases, such as when infants react to NVP, when there are stock shortages, or when infants are anemic. For example, AZT may replace NVP in anemic infants, or triple ARV therapy may be initiated if the infant shows symptoms of HIV. Extended NVP prophylaxis for 12 weeks is recommended in cases where mothers did not receive ART before or during delivery or were newly diagnosed with HIV shortly after delivery. 4. HIV Testing for Infants: One country has successfully implemented virological testing (PCR) at birth, finding it feasible, while others anticipate significant challenges. Eight countries are conducting routine infant HIV testing at immunization and growth monitoring clinics, with varying levels of difficulty reported. 5. Training and Capacity Building: All 21 surveyed countries have conducted training on HIV and infant feeding, either as stand-alone courses or integrated into IYCF, HIV/PMTCT, or nutrition training. Most training programs have been updated since 2010, with recent sessions held in the majority of countries. Health workers trained include general doctors, HIV specialists, nurses, midwives, community health workers, and nutrition officers. Training on heat treatment of expressed breast milk is included in about half of the countries. 6. Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E): Breastfeeding practices are monitored through integrated M&E systems, often linked to child health, postnatal care, or PMTCT/HIV registers. Indicators such as early breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding, and replacement feeding are documented in most countries. Longitudinal follow-up of infant feeding practices is rare, with only half of the countries documenting such data. Data disaggregation by HIV status, age, sex, and feeding practices is common, but regular data collection from facilities is inconsistent. 7. Challenges in Implementation: Key challenges include shortages of resources (e.g., test kits, ARVs), weak M&E systems, adherence to ARVs, and follow-up of patients. Specific issues include working mothers unable to continue exclusive breastfeeding, economic barriers to purchasing infant formula, and lack of understanding or support for new policies among healthcare workers. Coordination between HIV, PMTCT, nutrition, IYCF, and reproductive health programs is often lacking. Some countries also report insufficient government leadership. 8. Suggestions for WHO Guideline Review: Respondents highlighted the need for clearer guidance on complementary feeding, support for working mothers, and strategies for situations with ARV shortages. They also suggested promoting continued breastfeeding until 24 months, providing operational guidance for family-centered care, and improving counseling and training materials. Recommendations included exploring more effective ARV regimens, introducing DNA-PCR testing at birth, and addressing financial barriers to implementation. 9. Conclusion: The evaluation of the 2010 HIV and infant feeding guidelines across 21 countries revealed progress but also highlighted inconsistencies in implementation. Areas such as complementary feeding, support for working mothers, and monitoring systems require further clarity and emphasis. Strong scientific evidence is critical to support new recommendations, particularly regarding continued breastfeeding beyond six months. These findings will inform the finalization of the 2015 guidelines.
